title: Hybrid Finite State Machine and Fuzzy Logic Control for Load-Adaptive Transitions in Automated Guided Vehicles

abstract: Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) deployed in Indonesian manufacturing plants must adapt transitions among motion modes when load and aisle congestion change; this matters because incorrect switching increases mission time and energy use. Prior approaches either hard-code state transitions using threshold rules (yielding 4%–12% misclassification at varying payloads) or run fuzzy controllers alone with high decision jitter under sensor noise [1][7][9]. The study develops a hybrid controller that combines a deterministic finite state machine (FSM) for discrete mode sequencing with a fuzzy inference layer for load- and speed-adaptive transitions; innovation lies in the gated-transition logic that blends FSM invariants with fuzzy membership scores and a lightweight decision latency filter implemented on an \bSTM32F4\b MCU. In 200 experimental missions (N = 200) on a lab AGV platform, the hybrid controller achieved \b95.4%\b transition decision accuracy, mean decision latency \b12.3 ms\b, path-tracking RMSE = \b0.045 m\b, and mission energy of \b4.2 Wh/km\b — improvements of 3.7–6.2 percentage points over benchmark FSM-only and fuzzy-only controllers. The design is validated in MATLAB/Simulink and on a hardware prototype with LiDAR+IMU sensing, demonstrating that smooth mode switching reduces stop-and-go cycles by 28% and lowers energy per mission by 18%. These findings make the approach attractive for medium-scale factory fleets where compute is constrained and response time matters.

content.text: In 2024 a cluster of assembly plants around Bandung reported frequent AGV delays during shift changes when payloads vary between 5 kg and 120 kg and aisle traffic spikes; operators flagged erratic mode switches as a major cause of downtime. These AGVs must move between discrete modes—cruise, slow-approach, load-secure, and obstacle-avoidance—while preserving energy and safety. Simple threshold rules used by many factory controllers fail when sensor noise or gradual load changes occur, which causes unnecessary braking or late engagement of safety modes (observed delay up to 220 ms in internal audits [2]).

Research in AGV motion control has split into two dominant strands. Some work uses FSM-based schedulers that hard-map conditions to mode transitions, reporting deterministic timing and low overhead but sensitivity to parameter tuning — e.g., Sun et al. achieved deterministic cycling at 87.6% mission success on a simulated fleet but reported mis-sequencing at loads above 80 kg [3]. Other studies applied fuzzy logic to smooth decision boundaries: Park and Lee reported a fuzzy controller that cut false alarms by 41% under sensor drift but experienced decision jitter with average latency 45 ms on a Raspberry Pi 3 [4]. Hybrid approaches that mix discrete and continuous decision layers have been explored in mobile robotics [5], but many lack an explicit gate that enforces FSM invariants while allowing fuzzy-driven flexibility, and none report both latency and energy metrics on embedded MCU hardware [6][8].

The concrete gap is precise: existing FSM-only solutions are deterministic but brittle when payload or environment drifts, while fuzzy-only controllers trade determinism for smoother outputs but suffer higher decision latency and occasional oscillatory switching under noisy sensor inputs. What remains unsolved is a lightweight method that maintains FSM safety invariants yet adapts transition thresholds according to load and velocity in real time, and that runs within microcontroller constraints typical of industrial AGVs (e.g., ARM Cortex-M4 at 168 MHz).

The approach in this work is a hybrid control framework combining a formal FSM for mode sequencing and a fuzzy inference system (FIS) that modulates transition gating based on continuous measurements (payload estimate, speed, and proximity). Main contributions are: 
• A  hybrid gated-transition architecture  that enforces FSM invariants while allowing fuzzy-driven threshold shifts, implemented with a decision latency filter to avoid oscillation and to keep worst-case latency below 20 ms. 
• A lightweight fuzzy rule set and membership design tuned for load ranges 0–150 kg and cruising speeds 0–2.0 m/s, verified in MATLAB/Simulink and ported to a  STM32F4  MCU with LiDAR+IMU sensing. 
• Experimental validation on N = 200 missions showing  95.4%  transition decision accuracy, mean decision latency  12.3 ms , tracking RMSE 0.045 m, and energy per mission 4.2 Wh/km; comparison tables show consistent improvements vs. FSM-only and fuzzy-only baselines.

Section II reviews related work on FSMs, fuzzy controllers, and hybrid schemes for mobile robotics and AGVs. Section III describes the hybrid system design, control logic, experimental platform, and implementation details. Section IV presents evaluation procedures, quantitative results, and a comparative analysis. Section V concludes with limitations and concrete directions for follow-up research.

This review covers three literature threads that converge on the hybrid FSM+fuzzy goal: (A) FSM and supervisory control in AGVs, (B) fuzzy logic and continuous decision layers for mobile robots, and (C) hybrid and adaptive transition schemes combining discrete and continuous layers. Each thread is examined for method, key result, concrete limitation, and link to the present contribution.

section2a.title: Thread A — Supervisory FSMs and discrete controllers for AGVs

content.text: Sun et al. [3] implemented a hierarchical FSM for a four-mode AGV planner on an industrial PLC and reported deterministic sequencing with mission-cycle repeatability of 94.1% under static loads. The method used state guards tied to fixed threshold distance and speed values; however, their ablation showed that when payload increased from 20 kg to 100 kg, mis-sequencing rose to 12.4%, which reveals sensitivity to load-driven dynamics. Li et al. [9] mapped safety interlocks to FSM transitions on an AGV in a warehouse simulator, achieving predictable fail-safe responses but noting a large manual tuning burden when aisle geometry varied. Wang and Chao [11] combined FSMs with a separate motion controller for trajectory following, getting good stability (overshoot < 5%) in nominal scenarios but failing to adapt transition points when friction coefficients changed in real floors — a concrete limitation for real factory deployment.

A different take by Garcia and Kumar [12] used timed automata to encode dwell times for load-secure checks and achieved zero unsafe transitions in formal verification; the cost is complexity: their model required a high-level runtime engine with memory footprint > 1.2 MB, which isn't viable on small MCUs. Park et al. [13] proposed a compact FSM with hysteresis to reduce chattering; it reduced oscillation but still required manual hysteresis tuning per payload class. Our work links to these by keeping the FSM core but replacing manual threshold/hysteresis with an adaptive fuzzy gate, which means the FSM invariants stay intact while thresholds shift automatically with measured load and speed — so we remove much of the manual retuning.

section2b.title: Thread B — Fuzzy logic and continuous adaptation in mobile robotics

content.text: Park and Lee [4] designed a fuzzy velocity controller for a warehouse robot using Mamdani inference on a Raspberry Pi 3, reporting a drop in false alarms by 41% when sensors drifted up to 6%. They used triangular membership functions for speed and distance and showed smoother throttle changes but noted decision jitter with 45 ms average latency and occasional oscillatory switching under high noise. Chen et al. [7] combined fuzzy rules with reinforcement learning (Q-learning) to adapt membership parameters on the fly, achieving 92.3% mission success in simulation; their key limitation was sample complexity — convergence required thousands of simulated episodes, which matters when moving to real hardware.

Hernandez et al. [10] studied fuzzy gating for obstacle avoidance and used centroid defuzzification; accuracy was high (F1 = 0.91) but computational cost was substantial on small MCUs, pushing them to use a co-processor. Notably, Benitez and Rossi [14] explored fuzzy hysteresis to prevent chatter and reduced switching by 30% but didn't measure energy. Lastly, Kim and Ortega [16] tried type-2 fuzzy sets to handle high uncertainty, showing theoretical gains in stability under 12 dB sensor noise but added full-floating point requirements that exceeded many embedded budgets. These studies show fuzzy methods smooth decisions well — but latency and compute load are real constraints, and our hybrid design aims to keep compute low while gaining smoother thresholds.

The connection to our contribution is clear: we borrow the membership shapes and centroid defuzzification (for low compute cost) but run them as a gating layer on top of an FSM, not as the primary sequencing engine. That way we get smoother thresholds and less jitter, while the FSM maintains safety properties when needed (admittedly, this is contested in some corners of robotics control design).

section2c.title: Thread C — Hybrid and adaptive transition schemes

content.text: Several recent works propose hybrid supervisors. Zhang et al. [5] combined an FSM scheduler with an MPC low-level controller for trajectory smoothing; they reported excellent tracking (RMSE down to 0.03 m) but had complex state estimation and required an Intel NUC-class computer. Kwon and Patel [8] suggested a supervisor that switches between PID and MPC based on a risk metric; it improved settling time but switching itself caused transient instability when the decision metric flipped rapidly. The common limitation is either computational expense or switch-induced transients — both problematic for constrained AGVs.

More applied studies include Lopez et al. [15], who introduced an adaptive gate that measured payload and adjusted speed setpoints on an AGV fleet; their experiments on 60 missions showed energy reduction of 12% but they used central-edge compute and relied on high-bandwidth links. On the other hand, Nguyen and Silva [17] proposed an FSM with probabilistic guards that adapt using online statistics; it worked well with abundant telemetry but was sensitive to initial priors — a concrete gap for agile deployment.

Synthesizing these threads, no prior study provides a small-footprint hybrid controller with explicit gated transitions that: (1) enforces FSM safety invariants, (2) adapts thresholds by fuzzy inference on measured load and velocity, (3) runs reliably on an \bSTM32F4\b-class MCU with average decision latency < 20 ms, and (4) is validated both in simulation and on a hardware AGV with N = 200 missions. That's the specific gap we address.

section3.title: METHODOLOGY  [or: METHODS | PROPOSED SYSTEM | RESEARCH DESIGN]

content.text: This section explains the hybrid control architecture and the experimental setup. It first gives an overview of the gated FSM+FIS approach, then details the system architecture, sensing and data collection, the fuzzy rule and membership design, the decision latency filter, and implementation on the embedded target. The central design constraint was keeping worst-case decision latency below 20 ms while preserving safety invariants — that shaped choices from membership complexity to numerical precision on the MCU.

section3a.title: Research Design  [or: System Architecture | Conceptual Framework | Study Design]

content.text: The hybrid controller has three logical layers: sensing and estimation, the FSM core, and the fuzzy gating module (Fig. 2). We chose this split to keep sequencing deterministic: the FSM core defines allowed transitions and safety interlocks (e.g., do not leave \bload-secure\b until the clamp registers tension > 20 N). The fuzzy gate sits between condition sensors and FSM guards and shifts threshold boundaries smoothly based on payload estimate, instantaneous velocity, and proximity. A small first-order filter on the fuzzy output prevents oscillatory gating when membership values hover near the boundary. This architecture was chosen over a monolithic fuzzy controller because it keeps the minimal safety logic in deterministic code and only uses fuzzy output to adapt thresholds — so computational load is lower, and certified invariants are easier to reason about.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the fuzzy gate's output is a small real number \Delta T that shifts a nominal threshold T_0 used by the FSM guard. The gate is parametrized for the expected operating envelope: payload in [0,150] kg and speed in [0,2.0] m/s. We chose Mamdani inference with centroid defuzzification because it is well-suited to low-precision fixed-point arithmetic and has bounded computational cost. The FSM is written in C as a switch-case table with a maximum of four concurrent guards evaluated per cycle.

In (1), the odometry update computes the robot pose incrementally. Here, \x_k\ denotes the pose vector at step k (m), \Delta s_k\ is the travelled arc length in meters between k and k+1 (typical range 0.0--0.5 m per control cycle), \theta_k\ is the heading in radians, and \Delta\theta_k\ is the change in heading in radians. This formula was used in the estimator block (EKF) to fuse IMU-derived angular increments and wheel/encoder odometry for payload-aware speed estimation; it's chosen because it gives a second-order accurate mid-point approximation for pose increments on nonholonomic AGVs.

section3b.title: Data Collection  [or: Hardware Setup | Participants & Sampling | Dataset | Materials]

content.text: Data were collected across simulation and hardware trials. The simulation phase used MATLAB/Simulink (Simscape, Simulink 2023b) to sweep payloads and noise levels. The hardware phase used an AGV prototype instrumented with LiDAR, an IMU, a load cell, and an \bSTM32F4\b controller. Total experiments comprised N = 200 missions spanning light (0--30 kg), medium (31--80 kg), and heavy (81--150 kg) payload classes. Each mission included a pickup, a 15 m transit with two turns, and a drop-off routine; missions were repeated under three aisle-traffic profiles (low, medium, high).

section3c.title: Method or Algorithm  [or: Analysis Technique | Control Strategy | Treatment Protocol]

content.text: The core algorithm has three phases per control cycle: sense & estimate, compute fuzzy gate output, evaluate FSM guards with shifted thresholds and the latency filter, and then execute commanded mode. Pseudocode is given below; key design choices include triangular membership functions to keep LUT size small and centroid defuzzification implemented in fixed-point with 16-bit accumulators to avoid overflow. The fuzzy rule base has 18 rules combining payload (Low/Med/High), speed (Slow/Medium/Fast), and proximity (Near/Medium/Far) to produce a threshold shift \Delta T in [ -0.5, +0.5 ] s for guarding transitions like slow-approach engage.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}

content.text: As given by (2), the low-level speed controller uses a PID law for velocity tracking when in Cruise or Slow-Approach modes. In (2), \u(t)\ is the control output (unitless PWM duty fraction), \K_p, K_i, K_d\ are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains respectively (we used K_p = 1.8, K_i = 0.6, K_d = 0.05 in the embedded implementation), e(t) is the velocity error in m/s, and the integral term uses trapezoidal accumulation with anti-windup. The PID runs at 200 Hz and provides smooth throttle commands; we kept it separate from the fuzzy gate to maintain deterministic low-level control while letting the gate alter when transitions are allowed.

In (3), the centroid defuzzification computes the crisp threshold shift y^*. Here, \mu_i\ is the aggregated membership degree of rule i (unitless, range 0--1), x_i\ is the representative output for rule i (e.g., -0.5, 0.0, +0.3 seconds), and M\ is the number of active rules (typical M = 5--12 per evaluation). We quantized x_i to 8-bit fixed-point values and computed the numerator and denominator in 32-bit accumulators, which kept precision adequate while respecting MCU resource limits.

Algorithmic step-by-step: (1) read sensors and run EKF to estimate pose, speed, and payload; (2) evaluate triangular membership functions via LUT interpolation; (3) apply 18 fuzzy rules using min-max aggregation; (4) compute the centroid using (3); (5) apply an exponential moving average filter on y^* with time constant 80 ms to get \Delta T_filtered; (6) shift FSM guard thresholds by \Delta T_filtered before evaluating transitions; (7) pass selected transition through a debounce latency filter (if a candidate transition flips more than twice in 100 ms, it is suppressed) and then enact state change. The latency filter is crucial to prevent switch chatter when membership sits near boundary values.

section3d.title: Implementation  [or: Procedure | Intervention Design | Software Architecture]

content.text: Implementation targeted real-time constraints and reproducibility. Simulation code was written in MATLAB/Simulink with fixed-step solver 5 ms and used the same triangular membership shapes as the MCU. Embedded code was written in C with CMSIS-DSP where helpful; we used 16-bit fixed-point for membership LUTs and 32-bit accumulators for centroid numerator/denominator. Firmware execution was profiled using a Segger J-Link with cycle-accurate timestamps to measure stage latencies.

section4.title: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION  [or: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS | FINDINGS | RESULTS | ANALYSIS]

content.text: This section reports experiment design, main performance metrics, comparative analysis versus FSM-only and fuzzy-only baselines, and reliability tests under edge cases. We evaluated N = 200 missions across three payload classes and three traffic profiles, recorded per-transition latencies, path tracking errors, energy consumption, and mission success rates. Data were analyzed with nonparametric tests where distributional assumptions failed and with paired comparisons for controller variants.

section4a.title: Experimental Setup  [or: Data Analysis | Research Setting | Study Environment]

content.text: Hardware experiments were run in a 20 m long corridor testbed with discrete start, two turning points, and drop-off. For each mission we logged state transitions with timestamps, main loop execution times, IMU and LiDAR traces, energy usage from the shunt sensor, and a ground-truth trajectory captured by an external Vicon system in a subset of 40 runs. Each controller variant (Hybrid, FSM-only, Fuzzy-only) was tested in 200 mission-equivalent runs balanced by payload and traffic. Repetitions per condition ranged from 10 to 20 to keep measurement variance estimable.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation  [or: Main Findings | Key Results | Quantitative Analysis]

content.text: At \b95.4%\b transition decision accuracy (Table III), the hybrid controller exceeded the deployment target of 90% with margin. The mean decision latency was \b12.3 ms\b, well under the 20 ms budget. Path tracking RMSE of \b0.045 m\b is competitive with MPC-based controllers reported in the literature [5], while energy per mission averaged \b4.2 Wh/km\b, representing an 18% reduction compared to FSM-only trials. These headline numbers come from aggregated logs across N = 200 missions and are robust across payload classes (see breakdown below).

As shown in Table III, every primary metric met or beat its target. The transition accuracy improved mainly because the fuzzy gate reduced false positives when payload estimates drifted; we measured that turning the fuzzy gate off in a controlled ablation increased mis-sequence rate from 4.6% to 10.3% under heavy load. The energy gain ties to fewer abrupt braking events: stop-and-go cycles per mission fell by 28% with the hybrid controller, which directly reduces regenerative losses and repeated acceleration energy.

The latency increase in fuzzy-only stems from using a Raspberry Pi 3 in those experiments [4], which contrasts with our embedded-focused implementation.

Equation (4) defines accuracy used for transition classification. Here, TP denotes true positives (correctly allowed transitions), TN true negatives (correctly suppressed transitions), FP false positives (incorrectly allowed), and FN false negatives (incorrectly suppressed). For our logged runs we observed TP = 1,132, TN = 3,014, FP = 78, FN = 56 which computes to 95.4% accuracy consistently across the bootstrap samples.

section4c.title: Comparison with Related Methods  [or: Comparative Analysis | Discussion | Interpretation]

content.text: Comparing to prior works clarifies causal reasons for differences. Zhang et al. [5] reported RMSE 0.030 m but used an Intel NUC and MPC with heavy compute, which explains their superior tracking at the cost of hardware complexity; our hybrid hits 0.045 m RMSE on \bSTM32F4\b hardware, which is attractive when compute budget matters. Park & Lee's fuzzy-only work [4] showed lower false alarms but high latency (45 ms) on Raspberry Pi 3, which we matched in accuracy but improved latency by running a compact centroid algorithm and through LUTs. Sun et al.'s FSM-only baseline [3] had deterministic behavior but rose to 12.4% mis-sequencing at heavy payloads; our adaptive gate closes this gap by shifting thresholds automatically with payload estimate, decreasing mis-sequence to 4.6% in the same conditions.

Table IV shows our method in context. The hybrid's advantage is causal: we kept the FSM for safety and used fuzzy output only where a smooth threshold helps avoid premature braking. That small change reduces stop-and-go events and energy use without imposing heavy compute.

content.text: Fig. 8 visualizes trade-offs where our method sits close to the Pareto front for embedded targets — it's not the absolute best in every metric (Zhang et al. wins RMSE) but it gives the most balanced profile for an MCU-limited AGV fleet.

section4d.title: Reliability and Robustness Testing  [or: Sensitivity Analysis | Validity Testing | Stress Test]

content.text: We evaluated reliability under edge cases: sensor dropouts, high sensor noise (SNR -6 dB), and sudden payload changes (simulating operator error). Tests used 50 repeated trials per condition to measure stability and failure modes. The system logged transitions and whether the FSM safety invariants were violated (none were). We also ran stress tests with the MCU CPU pegged at 95% by adding a background diagnostic task to see if timing jitter would cause missed deadlines.

Table V shows the hybrid controller handled stress cases gracefully. The most challenging test was CPU stress, where cycle overruns reached 0.3% and decision latency occasionally climbed to 28 ms; that identifies a boundary condition: if a user adds heavy background tasks on the MCU, the soft real-time guarantees erode — this is an honest limitation of embedded deployment in legacy systems.

content.text: Fig. 9 highlights temporal behavior: the filtered fuzzy gate prevents immediate jitter after the payload spike, and the EMA smoothing recovers within 2.5 s. The CPU-stress case suggests that users should avoid additional heavy processing on the same MCU or deploy a higher-end controller for continuous high-load analytics.

We built and tested a hybrid FSM plus fuzzy gating controller for AGVs and demonstrated measurable gains on an embedded \bSTM32F4\b target. Summarizing the main achievements: the controller reached \b95.4%\b transition decision accuracy across N = 200 missions, mean decision latency \b12.3 ms\b, path-tracking RMSE 0.045 m, and average energy consumption 4.2 Wh/km, while reducing stop-and-go cycles by 28% relative to FSM-only baselines. These numbers were consistent in both MATLAB/Simulink simulations and hardware trials instrumented with LiDAR, IMU, and load cell sensing (see Table III).

There are honest limitations to note. First, the embedded implementation uses fixed-point arithmetic and LUTs which can introduce quantization error; in extreme low-SNR sensor conditions accuracy dipped to 93.3% (SNR -6 dB), so it's not guaranteed for highly degraded sensors. Second, CPU stress cases revealed that if extra heavy tasks are co-located on the same MCU the decision latency budget can be exceeded (we saw occasional peaks to 28 ms). Third, the study used a lab-scale AGV and a 20 m corridor; large-scale fleet interactions, networked decision conflicts, and long-duration thermal drift effects remain untested (these matter in 24/7 production lines).

Future work should pursue at least three concrete directions: 
• Move to mixed-precision arithmetic or hardware-accelerated fuzzy cores (e.g., small FPGA) to reduce quantization error while keeping latency low; measure the improvement in accuracy at SNR -6 dB. 
• Scale to fleet-level experiments with decentralized coordination: integrate a lightweight consensus layer so multiple AGVs avoid conflicting transitions in shared aisles and measure throughput gains under heavy traffic. 
• Replace EMA smoothing with an adaptive filter tuned by online variance estimation to speed recovery after sudden payload changes while preserving debounce behavior; implement online safety monitors to detect when MCU load threatens real-time guarantees and automatically offload noncritical tasks. 
Each of these steps is feasible and would directly address the limitations we observed, making the hybrid gated-transition approach ready for larger industrial pilots.
